body_markdown:
At Roku, we continually work on protecting our developer machines and build servers (CI runners) from a troubling new trend: attackers slipping malicious code into popular open-source packages so that installing the package runs a script that quietly steals your credentials. If you’ve tried to defend against this, you’ve probably hit the same wall we did. The usual tools don’t quite fit:


**Linux security frameworks like SELinux and AppArmor** **Process sandboxes like Landlock, bubblewrap, and firejail**


**Secrets managers**


can lock down almost anything, but writing a rule as simple as “ *only these five programs may read my SSH keys* ” means authoring more security policy than the problem is worth. are great for isolating one program at a time, but they don’t give you a persistent, machine-wide list of “ *these files and environment variables are off-limits to anything untrusted.* “ solve how secrets are stored and rotated, but once a malicious install script is already running with your real` GH_TOKEN` or AWS keys loaded in memory, it’s too late.


The pattern behind the 2025–26 supply-chain worms (Shai-Hulud, ChainDrop, Miasma, TeamPCP, the Keyv family, and others) is actually simple: a malicious install script walks the usual places secrets live, dotfiles, SSH keys, or environment variables, and ships them off. Two tools, dirblock and envblock, were built to stop exactly that pattern.


---


# The real-world impact


These aren’t theoretical attacks. Over the past twelve months, the same credential-harvest pattern has landed again and again, across npm and PyPI, through hijacked maintainer accounts, typosquats, and self-spreading worms. Each time it arrived at a scale that would have been hard to imagine a few years ago, with billions of downloads affected.


When Campaign What happened Scale


September 2025[Shai-Hulud](https://reversinglabs.com/blog/new-shai-hulud-worm-spreads-what-to-know) first self-propagating npm worm; credential theft + republish. 180–500 packages, ~2.6B combined weekly downloads


November–December 2025[Shai-Hulud 2.0](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/) expanded worm; hit maintainer accounts behind several widely used developer-tooling projects. ~800 packages


March 2026[npm HTTP client maintainer hijack](https://www.herodevs.com/blog-posts/the-axios-compromise-what-happened-what-it-means-and-what-you-should-do-right-now) hijacked maintainer account; two malicious versions published, with a postinstall script in a new dependency installing a cross-platform remote-access trojan. ~100M weekly downloads


April 2026[Credential-manager CLI typosquat](https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/blog/cloud-security/bitwardencli-supply-chain-attack/) typosquat impersonating a legitimate CLI; credential theft + worm propagation. Thousands of downloads before flagged


May 2026[Mini Shai-Hulud](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/shai-hulud-chaindrop-npm-supply-chain) preinstall scripts; stole tokens then self-propagated. 170+ packages, high weekly downloads


June 2026[Miasma / Hades](https://www.securityweek.com/over-100-npm-pypi-packages-hit-in-new-shai-hulud-supply-chain-attacks/) multi-stage droppers scanning local + cloud credentials. 100+ npm/PyPI packages


August 2026[CHAINDROP](https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/shai-hulud-chaindrop-npm-supply-chain) compromised maintainer → worm across co-owned packages. 400+ packages, >1.3B monthly downloads


The common thread: in nearly every incident, the damage happened in the first seconds of` npm install` or` pip install` , a package-manager lifecycle script, running as you, walking the usual places secrets live. That’s the specific gap dirblock and envblock were built to close.


## Malware campaign targets focus on secrets


Even today, a large percentage of malware attacks target secrets through environment variables and special directories. Developers are now under constant threat while updating packages.
Reporting on affected users and accounts is not well documented, but the number of campaigns grows


---


# dirblock+envblock: Targeted Protection


**dirblock** protects sensitive directories with “ **deny all except** ” trusted programs.


**envblock** protects sensitive environment variables with “ **deny all except** …”


## The tools


The solution is two small Linux daemons, each responsible for one half of the problem: protecting sensitive files, and neutralizing stolen environment variables.


**dirblock** (67 KB) — a fanotify` FAN_OPEN_PERM` daemon that mediates file opens. You declare sensitive directories and the short list of executables (plus optional ancestry profiles and cmdline filters) that are allowed to open them. Everything else is denied. Fails open by design: if the daemon stops, file opens aren’t mediated — intentional, so a crashed helper never locks engineers out of their own keys.


**envblock** (119 KB) — an eBPF program that sits on` execve` . Sensitive environment variables are delivered only when both the target executable and its entire ancestry chain are trusted (trust is by` mount_id + inode` , not by path). Untrusted children receive poisoned placeholder values. Never blocks execution; it just makes stolen secrets useless.


**They are intentionally narrow. They do not try to be a general MAC system.**


## Where these tools would have made the difference


The incidents above share one credential-harvest step: a lifecycle script scraping disk and environment during install. The table rates how dirblock + envblock would have mitigated that step, not the whole campaign.

## Efficacy against 2026 malware campaigns


By early October, dirblock and envblock would have fully blocked about 41% of the credential-stealing campaigns seen in 2026, and blocked or partially mitigated about 65%. The gap of roughly 25 points between the two lines is the partial cases: campaigns where the tools would have limited the damage without stopping it outright.


---


## Running them in practice


Most engineers who start hardening end up abandoning the effort because the tools demand continuous high-effort policy work. dirblock and envblock keep both the initial setup and the ongoing work small. Once running, all you maintain is a short allow-list for each tool, plus a reload when a trusted tool changes.


**67 KB + 119 KB**


Two small user-space daemons, plus a small eBPF program for envblock


**No kernel module**


Built from source; capabilities such as` cap_sys_admin` /` cap_bpf` applied with setcap.


**TOML config**


Generation scripts, ancestry helpers and a first-class dry-run mode


## Protect the secret, not every program


There are two ways to keep strangers out of a room. You can give everyone in the building a badge listing every room they may enter, or you can lock that one room and hand keys to the three people who need it.
SELinux and AppArmor work like the badges. Rules are written per program, so keeping a malicious install script out of` ~/.ssh` means profiling every program that might run during an install, and keeping those profiles current as tools change. dirblock and envblock work like the locked room. The rule guards the secret: you name the few programs allowed to touch it, and everything else is denied (dirblock) or handed a decoy value (envblock).
That’s what inverting the cost curve means: the work grows with the number of secrets you protect, not the number of programs on your machine.
**Goal:** only` ssh` ,` ssh-agent` and git may read` ~/.ssh` .


## Automatic config + “AI Ready”


Both tools ship markdown written for AI coding agents, and envblock includes an explicit` AI_HELPER.md` . If you already use Cursor, Claude, Codex or similar, the agent can help choose what to protect, generate test reports before you enforce, and keep the config current as your tools change. ## Trust is deliberately brittle


**Ancestry check.** Malware doesn’t have to steal your keys itself; it can get a trusted tool to do it. A malicious install script calls` git` , and` git` reads` ~/.ssh` on its behalf. Programs launch other programs, which launch others in turn, so every file open or` execve` comes with a chain of ancestors, and a tool such as AppArmor only looks at the last link:` git` is allowed to read` ~/.ssh` , so the theft goes through.
dirblock and envblock check the whole chain. If any link is untrusted, the request is denied (dirblock) or the secret is poisoned (envblock), even when the program making the request is on the allow-list. They ask not just who is reading the secret, but how it got there.


**Identity check.** The ancestry check asks how a program got there. A second check asks whether it’s still the same program. Trust is tied to the file itself, not its path (envblock identifies binaries by` mount_id + inode` ), so replacing an allow-listed binary, by an upgrade or by an attacker, leaves the new file untrusted until you reload.


---


## What they do not do


- They are not a replacement for package integrity, network egress controls, or proper secrets management.
- They fail open (dirblock) or poison instead of blocking (envblock).
- Memory scraping of a live process and network exfiltration by an already-trusted binary remain out of scope.
- envblock has hard eBPF verifier bounds (number of variables, env slots scanned, ancestry depth).


---


## Bottom line


If you have already evaluated the heavyweight options and decided the ongoing cost was too high for the protection you actually needed, these two tools sit in a useful gap. They are small, fast to stand up, stay out of the way of legitimate work, and raise the bar dramatically against the exact credential-harvest pattern that has dominated the last twelve months of supply-chain attacks.
While this article has focused on malicious packages that steal credentials at install time, dirblock and envblock also stop prompt-injected or overly curious AI coding agents from reading secrets they haven’t been granted.
